cards.text: Proverbs keeps rolling, and a father is still teaching his son, same as last chapter (Prov 4:1). He opens by telling his son to pay attention to his wisdom and lean in to his insight. Translation: phone DOWN, friend, Dad's got something important.

cards.question: Why does the father want his son listening so closely?

answers.text: To earn a seat with the elders
To grow rich before he is old

cards.text: Then he warns about the forbidden woman. Though her lips drip honey and her speech is smoother than oil, friend, that's a text that says CONGRATULATIONS YOU WON, and you never entered ANYTHING.

cards.question: The father says that in the end the forbidden woman is ___.
The father calls the forbidden woman bitter as wormwood and sharp as a double-edged sword. Where does he say her steps lead?
The forbidden woman carefully considers the path of life.

cards.text: She doesn't even know her ways are unstable. Reminds me of my first week on this gold base, hopping around like a PRO when I was really just a wobble with a mustache.
So now the father turns to "my sons" and tells them to listen and not turn aside from what he's saying.

cards.question: The father's game plan for dealing with the forbidden woman: keep your path ___ from her.

cards.text: Don't even go near the door of her house. That's me and the snooze button: if the phone's on the nightstand, I LOSE, so the phone sleeps across the room.

cards.question: The father warns that going near the forbidden woman could hand the son's years to someone cruel.
If the son goes near her door, who ends up feasting on his wealth?

cards.text: Then the father skips ahead to the end of the son's life. His flesh and his body are spent, and he groans.

cards.question: Groaning at the end of his life, what does the son finally admit?

answers.text: He hated discipline and ignored his teachers
He never had anyone to teach him
He worked too hard and rested too little

cards.question: The groaning son says he's on the brink of ruin all alone where nobody can see.

cards.text: Then the father switches pictures to water. He says, "Drink water from your own cistern, and running water from your own well."

cards.question: In the father's water picture, what is he telling the son to do?

answers.text: Stay with what is his own
Find his water in the city

cards.text: He asks, "Why should your springs flow in the streets, your streams of water in the public squares?" That's leaving your front door wide open with a sign that says HELP YOURSELF.

cards.question: The father says the son's streams of water should be shared with strangers.

cards.text: Then the father says may your fountain be blessed. And now the water picture gets personal.

cards.question: The father wishes that his son may rejoice in his ___.

cards.text: He calls her a loving doe, a graceful fawn, and says may you be captivated by her love forever. Friend, this isn't a lecture anymore, it's a WEDDING SPEECH.

cards.question: After wishing his son joy with the wife of his youth, what does the father ask him?

answers.text: Why be captivated by an adulteress
Why trust the advice of strangers
Why waste your years on hard work

cards.question: The father says the LORD sees only some of a man's paths.
The father finishes by talking about the wicked man. What traps him?

cards.text: The cords of his sin entangle him. That's me with a phone charger I tangled up MYSELF, yelling at a knot I tied.

cards.question: In the end, the wicked man dies for lack of ___.

cards.text: He's led astray by his own great folly. And there's that word again, discipline, the same one the groaning son said he hated.

findings.problem: Story cards 1 and 3 give away the answer to choice card 4 before it is asked. Card 1 quotes 'your own cistern... your own well.' Card 3 quotes the rhetorical 'Why should your springs flow in the streets...?' and adds the HELP YOURSELF joke. That leaves no doubt that the streams should not be shared with strangers, so the true or false on 5:17 tests nothing.

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

findings.problem: The question asks where her 'steps' lead and gives 'Down to death' as the answer. In Proverbs 5:5, it is her feet that go down to death. Her steps lead straight to Sheol. The card swaps what the text says.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: The joke is packed into the Bible fact's own sentence: 'Though her lips drip honey and her speech is smoother than oil, friend, that's a text that says CONGRATULATIONS YOU WON...' The 'though' clause sets up a contrast that never comes. Instead the scam-text image becomes its main clause, so the verse and the comparison blend into one broken sentence. The verse and the joke should be separate sentences.

rule.text: One image only. Never blend the comparison with the Bible setting.

findings.problem: Several jokes give Papa Dorin personal modern belongings and habits in the Dorinverse: a phone and a snooze button on his nightstand (stop 1 card 10), and a phone charger he tangled himself (stop 2 card 11). papa-dorin.md lets him use everyday adult life for comparisons, and lets his jokes make up small moments and habits around his bakery. It also says he never adds anything new to his own world. It doesn't say whether he can claim to own and use modern items like these himself.
findings.question: In his self-deprecating jokes, can Papa Dorin say he personally owns and uses modern items like a phone, snooze alarm, nightstand or phone charger? Or must everyday-life comparisons stay general, like 'that's like hitting snooze,' without placing those items in his own life?
